\begin{annexitem}{annex:p2.3.9}{thm:p02-interpolant-truth-table-correctness}{Correctness of the truth-table interpolant construction}
\begin{proof}
Let \(\theta\) be the output and let \(X\) be the common-variable set.  If a
valuation \(v\) satisfies \(\varphi\), its restriction \(v|_X\) is among the
selected assignments, so \(v\) satisfies the corresponding complete
conjunction and hence \(\theta\).  Thus
\(\varphi\entails\theta\).

Suppose instead that some valuation \(v\) satisfies \(\theta\) and falsifies
\(\psi\).  It satisfies a selected conjunction, whose assignment
\(u:X\to\{0,1\}\) therefore extends to a valuation \(w\) satisfying
\(\varphi\).  Amalgamate \(w\) on the variables occurring only in
\(\varphi\), \(v\) on those occurring only in \(\psi\), and their common
value \(u\) on \(X\).  The resulting valuation satisfies \(\varphi\) and
falsifies \(\psi\), contrary to the hypothesis.  Hence
\(\theta\entails\psi\).  By construction, every variable of \(\theta\) lies
in \(X\).  The empty selected family gives \(\bottom\), and an empty
conjunction gives \(\topv\), so the boundary cases obey the same argument.
\end{proof}
\end{annexitem}

\begin{hbtheorem}{thm:p02-two-sat}{cited=AspvallPlassTarjan1979}{2-SAT tractability}
For a 2-CNF instance without an empty clause, form the implication graph on
literals by adding directed edges from \(\overline L\) to \(K\) and from
\(\overline K\) to \(L\) for every clause \(L\lor K\), treating a unit clause
\(L\) as \(L\lor L\).  The instance
is satisfiable iff no occurring variable \(p\) has both \(p\) and \(\neg p\)
in one strongly connected component.  The test runs in \(O(N)\) time.
\end{hbtheorem}

\begin{hbdefinition}{def:p10-lindenbaum-algebra}{Lindenbaum--Tarski algebra}
For a propositional calculus \(S\) whose provable equivalence is a
congruence for its connectives, define
\(\varphi\equiv_S\psi\) when
\(S\vdash\varphi\leftrightarrow\psi\). The quotient of formulas by this
congruence, with connectives inducing operations, is the
\emph{Lindenbaum--Tarski algebra} of \(S\). The name is needed to distinguish a
syntactic quotient from an arbitrary Boolean algebra. It stands as an algebra
presented by formulas, differs because equality is provable equivalence, and
is used to turn maximal consistent theories into ultrafilters.
\index{Lindenbaum--Tarski algebra}
\end{hbdefinition}

\begin{hbdefinition}{def:p02-uniform-substitution}{Substitution, uniform@Uniform substitution}
A \emph{uniform substitution}\index{formula instance} is a function
\(\upsilon:\mathsf{Prop}\to\mathsf{Fm}_{\mathsf{CPL}}\).  Its instance map is
defined recursively by
\[
 p_n[\upsilon]=\upsilon(p_n),\quad \bottom[\upsilon]=\bottom,\quad
 (\neg\varphi)[\upsilon]=\neg(\varphi[\upsilon]),\quad
 (\varphi\circ\psi)[\upsilon]=
   (\varphi[\upsilon]\circ\psi[\upsilon]).
\]
\end{hbdefinition}

\begin{lemma}[Substitution for open assumptions]
\label{lem:nd-substitution}
If \(D\) derives \(\psi\) with an open assumption \(\varphi\), and \(E\)
derives \(\varphi\), then replacing each designated open occurrence of
\(\varphi\) in \(D\) by a copy of \(E\), after consistently renaming every
label in every copy to be globally fresh from \(D\) and from all other copies,
produces a derivation of \(\psi\).  Its open assumptions are those of \(D\)
other than the replaced occurrences, together with the correspondingly
renamed open assumptions of the inserted copies of \(E\).
\end{lemma}

\begin{theorem}[Substitution lemma]
\label{thm:fol-substitution}
For every formula \(\varphi\), term \(t\), variable \(x\), structure
\(\Meta\), and assignment \(s\),
\[
 \Meta,s\entails\varphi[t/x]
 \quad\text{iff}\quad
 \Meta,s[x\mapsto\sem{t}^{\Meta}_s]\entails\varphi.
\]
\end{theorem}

\begin{hbdefinition}{def:p10-modal-lindenbaum}{The normal modal Lindenbaum algebra}
Put
\[
 \varphi\equiv_L\psi
       \quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
       \vdash_L\varphi\leftrightarrow\psi.
\]
The following theorem verifies that this is a congruence.
Let \(F_L\) be the quotient of the formula algebra by this relation,
with classes \([\varphi]_L\) and induced operations
\[
\begin{gathered}
 0=[\bot]_L,\quad 1=[\top]_L,\quad
 \neg[\varphi]_L=[\neg\varphi]_L,\\
 [\varphi]_L\wedge[\psi]_L=[\varphi\wedge\psi]_L,\qquad
 \Box[\varphi]_L=[\Box\varphi]_L.
\end{gathered}
\]
This is the \emph{normal modal Lindenbaum algebra} of \(L\).
\index{Lindenbaum--Tarski algebra!normal modal logic}
\end{hbdefinition}

\begin{annexitem}{annex:p10.modal-algebra.1}{thm:p10-modal-algebra-completeness}{The modal quotient and algebraic completeness}
\begin{proof}
Classical propositional reasoning makes \(\equiv_L\) an
equivalence relation compatible with all Boolean connectives.
For the modal constructor, if
\(\vdash_L\varphi\leftrightarrow\psi\), then both implications
are theorems.  Necessitate each and apply distribution to obtain
\[
 \vdash_L\Box\varphi\to\Box\psi,\qquad
 \vdash_L\Box\psi\to\Box\varphi.
\]
Their conjunction yields
\(\vdash_L\Box\varphi\leftrightarrow\Box\psi\).
The quotient operations are therefore well-defined.
Boolean identities hold because their formula counterparts are
propositional tautologies.

The formula \(\Box\top\) is a theorem by necessitation.
Necessitating the two projections of a conjunction and applying
distribution proves
\(\Box(\varphi\wedge\psi)\to
(\Box\varphi\wedge\Box\psi)\).
For the converse, necessitate
\(\varphi\to(\psi\to\varphi\wedge\psi)\) and apply
distribution twice.
Thus \(\Box\) preserves \(1\) and binary meets in \(F_L\).
Taking Boolean duals shows that \(\Diamond\) preserves
\(0\) and binary joins.
This proves that \(F_L\) is a normal modal algebra.

Classical tautologies also give
\[
 [\chi]_L=1\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad\chi\in L:
\]
each of \(\chi\) and \(\chi\leftrightarrow\top\) implies
the other by propositional reasoning.
Induction on formulas gives
\[
 \llbracket\chi\rrbracket_\nu^{F_L}=[\chi]_L,
 \qquad \nu(p)=[p]_L.
\]

\paragraph{All valuations in the quotient.}
Fix \(\lambda\in L\) and an arbitrary valuation
\(v:\mathsf{Prop}\to F_L\).
Only finitely many variables occur in \(\lambda\).
For each of those variables \(p\), select a formula \(\rho_p\)
with \([\rho_p]_L=v(p)\).
Define a substitution \(\sigma\) by these finitely many choices,
and put \(\sigma(q)=q\) on all other variables.
Induction on the subformulas of \(\lambda\) gives
\[
 \llbracket\lambda\rrbracket_v^{F_L}=[\sigma(\lambda)]_L.
\]
Uniform-substitution closure puts \(\sigma(\lambda)\) in \(L\),
so this value is \(1\).
This proves \(F_L\in\operatorname{Alg}(L)\).
There was no selection of representatives for a whole infinite
family of equivalence classes.

If \(\varphi\notin L\), its value under \(\nu\) is not \(1\),
so \(F_L\) refutes it.  Conversely, every member of \(L\)
is valid in every member of \(\operatorname{Alg}(L)\) by
definition.  These statements prove all displayed equivalences.

The algebra definition also respects the stated normal-logic rules.
Meet preservation makes \(\Box_A\) monotone, and
\[
 \Box_A(a\to b)\wedge\Box_Aa
       =\Box_A((a\to b)\wedge a)\leq\Box_Ab
\]
proves distribution.
Modus ponens preserves validity, substitution is composition
with formula evaluation, and theorem necessitation preserves
validity because \(\Box_A1=1\).
Thus, if \(L\) is presented by additional axioms, validating
those axioms in a normal modal algebra validates every theorem.

If \(\bot\in L\), propositional explosion gives every formula
in \(L\); hence every two formulas are equivalent and \(F_L\)
is trivial.  Conversely, a trivial quotient has
\([\bot]_L=1\), so \(L\) is inconsistent.
Any algebra validating this logic must have \(0=1\);
the trivial modal algebras do validate every formula.
\end{proof}
\end{annexitem}

\begin{hbtheorem}{thm:p02-arbitrary-prop-completeness}{cited=HowardRubin1998}{Choice-calibrated propositional completeness}
Over \(\mathsf{ZF}\), the Boolean Prime Ideal Theorem proves: for every set
\(P\), set \(\Gamma\subseteq\operatorname{Form}(P)\), and formula \(\varphi\),
\[
 \Gamma\models\varphi\quad\Longrightarrow\quad
 \Gamma\vdash_{\mathsf{CPL}(P)}\varphi,
\]
where derivations remain finite and use only finitely many premises. In fact,
the corresponding unrestricted compactness/completeness scheme is equivalent
over \(\mathsf{ZF}\) to the Boolean Prime Ideal Theorem.
\end{hbtheorem}

\begin{hbtheorem}{thm:p02-fol-tableau-adequacy}{cited=Smullyan1968}{First-order tableau adequacy and countermodel extraction}
Let \(\Gamma\) be a finite set of equality-free \(\mathcal L\)-sentences.
Then \(\Gamma\) is unsatisfiable iff a finite closed tableau rooted at
\(\Gamma\) exists.  Moreover, for every fair saturated open branch \(B\),
define its positive atomic part by
\[
 B^{+}_{\mathrm{at}}
 \defeq
 \{R(t_1,\ldots,t_n):R(t_1,\ldots,t_n)\text{ occurs on }B\}.
\]
The corresponding Herbrand structure is
\(\mathcal M_{B^{+}_{\mathrm{at}}}\).  Its domain is the closed
\(\mathcal L_{\Gamma}^*\)-terms, its functions act by term formation, and
its relations are exactly the members of \(B^{+}_{\mathrm{at}}\).
The branch truth induction gives
\[
 \mathcal M_{B^{+}_{\mathrm{at}}}\entails B.
\]
Hence its
\(\mathcal L_{\Gamma}\)-reduct models \(\Gamma\), and interpreting every
unused \(\mathcal L\)-symbol arbitrarily expands it to an
\(\mathcal L\)-model of \(\Gamma\).
This is the countermodel-extraction clause, not merely a closure test.
\end{hbtheorem}

\begin{hbtheorem}{thm:p02-tableau-adequacy}{cited=Smullyan1968}{Tableau adequacy}
Let \(\Gamma\) be a finite set of propositional formulas.  Every closed
tableau rooted at \(\Gamma\) certifies that \(\Gamma\) is unsatisfiable.
Exhaustively expanding unmarked compound occurrences terminates in a finite
saturated tableau.  From any open saturated branch \(B\), define a valuation
by assigning a propositional variable \(p\) true exactly when \(p\) occurs
on \(B\) (and false otherwise).  This branch valuation satisfies every
formula on \(B\), hence every member of \(\Gamma\).  Consequently an
exhaustively expanded saturated tableau has an open branch
exactly when \(\Gamma\) is satisfiable, and it is closed exactly when
\(\Gamma\) is unsatisfiable.
\end{hbtheorem}

\begin{hbtheorem}{thm:p02-craig-interpolation}{cited=Craig1957}{Craig interpolation, sentence form}
Let \(\varphi\) and \(\psi\) be first-order sentences, possibly in different
signatures, and suppose \(\entails\varphi\to\psi\).  Then there is a sentence
\(\chi\) such that
\[
 \entails\varphi\to\chi,
 \qquad
 \entails\chi\to\psi,
\]
and every nonlogical constant, function symbol, and relation symbol occurring
in \(\chi\) occurs in both \(\varphi\) and \(\psi\).  When equality is logical,
it is exempt from the shared-vocabulary condition.
\index{Craig interpolation theorem}
\end{hbtheorem}

\begin{annexitem}{annex:p7.interp.3}{thm:craig-interpolation}{Craig interpolation}
\begin{proof}
\paragraph{The relational case.}
Let \(A,B\) be equality-free purely relational sentences with
\(\models A\to B\).
Theorem~\ref{thm:p07-relational-cut-free-completeness} supplies a
cut-free derivation of \(A\Rightarrow B\).
Put \(A\) in the first antecedent part and \(B\) in the second
succedent part of its partition.
Theorem~\ref{thm:p07-maehara-partition} supplies a sentence \(J\)
in the common predicate vocabulary, with derivations of
\(A\Rightarrow J\) and \(J\Rightarrow B\).
Soundness gives \(\models A\to J\) and \(\models J\to B\).
This establishes the relational case, including an empty common
predicate vocabulary.

\paragraph{A finite relational signature for each side.}
Now let \(A,B\) be arbitrary first-order sentences with
\(\models A\to B\).
Write \(\Sigma_1,\Sigma_2\) for their respective finite sets of
nonlogical symbols, with arities retained.
Only the union of these finite signatures is needed.
Every nonempty structure in that union extends to any unused
original symbols by assigning empty predicates and constant-valued
functions at one fixed element.

Introduce one fresh binary predicate \(E\).
For every \(m\)-ary function symbol \(f\), introduce a distinct
\((m+1)\)-ary predicate \(G_f\).  Thus a constant \(c\), regarded
as a function of arity zero, has a unary predicate \(G_c\).
Keep original predicate symbols unchanged.
The translated language is purely relational and has no logical
equality, functions, or constants.

For a finite signature \(\Sigma\), let \(\operatorname{Ax}_\Sigma\)
be the conjunction of the following finite set of relational sentences.
First require \(E\) to be an equivalence relation:
\[
\begin{gathered}
 \forall x\,E(x,x),\\
 \forall x\,y\,(E(x,y)\to E(y,x)),\\
 \forall x\,y\,z\,
       ((E(x,y)\land E(y,z))\to E(x,z)).
\end{gathered}
\]
For every original predicate in \(\Sigma\) and every graph predicate
associated with a function in \(\Sigma\), require congruence in all
coordinates.  For such a predicate \(H\) of arity \(r\geq1\), this is
\[
 \forall\bar x\,\bar y\,
 \left[
  \left(\bigwedge_{i=1}^{r}E(x_i,y_i)\right)
  \to\bigl(H(\bar x)\leftrightarrow H(\bar y)\bigr)
 \right].
\]
For arity zero, congruence is a tautology and is omitted.
Finally, for each \(m\)-ary function \(f\in\Sigma\), include
\[
\begin{aligned}
 &\forall x_1\cdots x_m\,\exists z\,
                   G_f(x_1,\ldots,x_m,z),\\
 &\forall x_1\cdots x_m\,z\,w\,
 \bigl((G_f(x_1,\ldots,x_m,z)\land
        G_f(x_1,\ldots,x_m,w))\to E(z,w)\bigr).
\end{aligned}
\]
For \(m=0\), the first sentence is \(\exists z\,G_c(z)\), and the
second is uniqueness modulo \(E\) for that unary graph.
The equivalence and conjunction symbols in these axioms have their
ordinary definitions in the selected primitives.
Only \(E\), original predicates from \(\Sigma\), and graphs of
functions from \(\Sigma\) occur in \(\operatorname{Ax}_\Sigma\).

\paragraph{Terms and formulas.}
For a term \(t\), define a relational formula \(V_t(z)\), where the
output variable \(z\) is fresh for \(t\), by
\[
\begin{aligned}
 V_x(z)&=E(x,z),\\
 V_{f(t_1,\ldots,t_m)}(z)
   &=\exists z_1\cdots z_m
       \left(\bigwedge_{i=1}^{m}V_{t_i}(z_i)
                       \land G_f(z_1,\ldots,z_m,z)\right).
\end{aligned}
\]
All auxiliary variables are distinct and fresh for the entire input
formula, and bound variables are renamed when necessary.
For a constant this gives \(V_c(z)=G_c(z)\).
The empty conjunction is \(\top\), and an empty existential block
does nothing.

The formula translation \((\cdot)^r\) fixes \(\bot\), commutes with
the Boolean connectives and quantifiers, and translates atoms by
\[
\begin{aligned}
 (P(t_1,\ldots,t_m))^r
  &=\exists z_1\cdots z_m
       \left(\bigwedge_{i=1}^{m}V_{t_i}(z_i)
                       \land P(z_1,\ldots,z_m)\right),\\
 (t=u)^r
  &=\exists z\,w\,
       (V_t(z)\land V_u(w)\land E(z,w)).
\end{aligned}
\]
A nullary atom is unchanged.
Every introduced variable is bound.  No original symbol is replaced
by the graph of a different symbol, so the translation preserves
which original side owns each predicate, function, or constant.

\paragraph{The quotient truth lemma.}
Let \(N\) be a nonempty relational structure satisfying
\(\operatorname{Ax}_\Sigma\), with domain \(D\).
Write \([a]\) for the \(E^N\)-class of \(a\in D\), and let \(Q\)
have domain \(D/E^N\).
Interpret an original predicate by
\[
 P^Q([a_1],\ldots,[a_m])
       \quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad N\models P(a_1,\ldots,a_m).
\]
Its congruence axiom makes this independent of the representatives.
Interpret \(f^Q([a_1],\ldots,[a_m])\) as the unique class \([b]\)
such that \(N\models G_f(a_1,\ldots,a_m,b)\).
Totality supplies a class, uniqueness makes it unique, and input
congruence makes it independent of the representatives of the inputs.
For constants the same clauses give a unique output class.
Logical equality in \(Q\) is identity of equivalence classes.

If \(s\) is an assignment into \(D\), write \(\bar s(x)=[s(x)]\).
Induction on a term proves
\[
 N,s[z:=a]\models V_t(z)
 \quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
 [a]=t^Q(\bar s).
\]
For a variable this is exactly the interpretation of \(E\).
For a function term, witnesses to the translated subterms give their
correct argument classes by induction, so its graph atom gives the
stated value class.  Conversely, choose representatives of the finitely
many argument classes.  Their term formulas hold by induction.
Totality gives a graph output in the required value class, and
congruence in the output coordinate permits replacement by the
specified representative \(a\).  This supplies all existential witnesses.
The constant case uses the same totality, uniqueness, and output
congruence with no arguments.

Induction on formulas now gives
\[
 N,s\models C^r
 \quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad Q,\bar s\models C.
\]
For an original predicate atom, the term lemma and predicate congruence
give both directions.  For equality, the term lemma identifies the
two value classes, and \(E\) says exactly that they agree.
Bottom and the Boolean connectives follow from their truth clauses.
For a quantifier, every value in \(D\) maps to an equivalence class,
and every class has a representative in \(D\).  Thus existential
witnesses lift and descend, and the universal quantifier ranges
over all classes exactly as required.  This proves the full truth lemma.

\paragraph{The interpolant uses only common symbols.}
Set \(\operatorname{Ax}_i=\operatorname{Ax}_{\Sigma_i}\).
We have the relational validity
\[
 \models(\operatorname{Ax}_1\land A^r)
                 \to(\operatorname{Ax}_2\to B^r).
\]
Indeed, a countermodel would satisfy both axiom conjunctions,
\(A^r\), and \(\neg B^r\).
Its quotient for \(\Sigma_1\cup\Sigma_2\) would satisfy
\(A\land\neg B\) by the truth lemma, contradicting the original
valid implication.
Apply the already proved relational case to these two sentences.
It gives a relational sentence \(J\) with
\[
\begin{aligned}
 &\models(\operatorname{Ax}_1\land A^r)\to J,\\
 &\models J\to(\operatorname{Ax}_2\to B^r).
\end{aligned}
\]
Its predicate vocabulary is contained in the intersection of the
two translated vocabularies.  Hence it can contain \(E\), common
original predicates, and \(G_f\) only for a function or constant
\(f\) occurring in both original sentences.

Decode \(J\) into a first-order sentence \(\theta\) by the atomic
replacements
\[
 E(x,y)\mapsto x=y,\qquad
 G_f(x_1,\ldots,x_m,z)\mapsto f(x_1,\ldots,x_m)=z,
\]
keeping original predicates and commuting with all logical operations.
For a constant the second replacement is \(G_c(z)\mapsto c=z\).
This introduces only common original symbols; equality is logical,
as permitted in the theorem.

For any original structure \(M\), its canonical relational expansion
\(M^r\) has the same domain, interprets \(E\) as actual equality,
and interprets each \(G_f\) as the graph of \(f^M\).
It satisfies both axiom conjunctions.
Its quotient is canonically isomorphic to \(M\), so the quotient
truth lemma yields \(M\models C\) iff \(M^r\models C^r\).
Also induction directly on \(J\) yields
\(M^r\models J\) iff \(M\models\theta\).
The first interpolant implication therefore gives
\(\models A\to\theta\); the second, since \(M^r\models
\operatorname{Ax}_2\), gives \(\models\theta\to B\).
This proves sentence interpolation in the general signature.

\paragraph{Free variables.}
Let now \(\varphi,\psi\) be formulas.
For each variable \(x\in\FV(\varphi)\cup\FV(\psi)\), choose a distinct
fresh constant symbol \(c_x\), and replace its free occurrences by
\(c_x\).  Let the resulting sentences be \(\varphi^c,\psi^c\).
Validity of \(\varphi\to\psi\) under every assignment implies
validity of \(\varphi^c\to\psi^c\) under every interpretation of the
new constants.
Sentence interpolation produces \(\theta^c\) with only common
symbols.  A constant \(c_x\) can therefore occur in it only when
\(x\in\FV(\varphi)\cap\FV(\psi)\).

Rename bound variables of \(\theta^c\) away from this finite set,
then replace each \(c_x\) by \(x\), including occurrences inside terms.
Call the result \(\theta\).
For any original structure and assignment \(s\), interpret
\(c_x\) as \(s(x)\).  Induction on terms and formulas identifies
the truth of \(\theta^c\) in this expansion with the truth of
\(\theta\) at \(s\), and likewise for the two input formulas.
The two sentence implications thus become
\(\models\varphi\to\theta\) and \(\models\theta\to\psi\).
The construction gives the asserted free-variable intersection.
Distinct new constant symbols were never required to denote
distinct elements, so this argument covers assignments with equal
values as well.
\end{proof}
\end{annexitem}

\begin{annexitem}{annex:p3.abstract.2}{thm:p03-beth-definability}{Beth definability theorem}
\begin{proof}
Let \(P'\) be a fresh predicate of the same arity \(n\) as \(P\), let
\(T'\) replace \(P\) by \(P'\) throughout \(T\), and leave every
symbol of \(\Lang\) unchanged.
Add distinct fresh constant symbols \(\bar c=(c_1,\ldots,c_n)\).
For arity zero, this tuple is empty.  If
\(T\cup\{P(\bar c)\}\) is inconsistent, then \(P\) is defined by
\(\bottom\); if \(T'\cup\{\neg P'(\bar c)\}\) is inconsistent, it is
defined by \(\neg\bottom\).
Indeed, the constants have arbitrary interpretations and do not occur
in \(T\); the first case forces \(P\) false on every tuple in every
\(T\)-model, and the second, after renaming back, forces it true.
Otherwise implicit definability makes
\[
 T\cup\{P(\bar c)\}\cup
 T'\cup\{\neg P'(\bar c)\}
\]
inconsistent: a model would give two expansions of one \(\Lang\)-reduct that
disagree on \(\bar c\).  The contrapositive of Robinson joint consistency
therefore gives a sentence \(\sigma(\bar c)\) in the common language
\(\Lang(\bar c)\) such that
\[
 T\cup\{P(\bar c)\}\entails\sigma(\bar c),
 \qquad
 T'\cup\{\neg P'(\bar c)\}\entails\neg\sigma(\bar c).
\]
The sentence \(\sigma(\bar c)\) contains neither \(P\) nor \(P'\).
The second entailment is classically equivalent to
\(T'\entails\sigma(\bar c)\to P'(\bar c)\).  Rename \(P'\) back to \(P\),
which leaves \(\sigma\) unchanged.  Together with the first entailment,
this gives \(T\models P(\bar c)\leftrightarrow\sigma(\bar c)\).

Choose distinct variables \(x_1,\ldots,x_n\), rename the bound variables
of \(\sigma\) away from them, and replace the fresh \(c_i\) by \(x_i\),
including occurrences inside terms.  Call the resulting formula
\(\theta(\bar x)\).
For every \(M\models T\) and every tuple \(\bar a\) in its domain,
interpret \(c_i\) by \(a_i\).  Substitution preserves truth under
this interpretation, so
\[
 M\models P(\bar a)\leftrightarrow\theta(\bar a).
\]
Different fresh constant symbols may denote equal elements, so this
argument covers all tuples.
Therefore
\[
 T\models\forall\bar x\,
                (P(\bar x)\leftrightarrow\theta(\bar x)),
 \qquad \FV(\theta)\subseteq\{x_1,\ldots,x_n\}.
\]
The same conclusion was established by the constant choices
\(\theta=\bot\) or \(\theta=\neg\bot\) in the two earlier cases.
It also covers an inconsistent \(T\).
For arity zero, it is simply the sentence \(P\leftrightarrow\theta\).

Apply the consequence form of first-order compactness,
Theorem~\ref{thm:fol-compactness}, to this one defining sentence.
It gives a finite \(T_0\subseteq T\) already entailing it, uniformly
for every model and tuple.
Completeness, Theorem~\ref{thm:fol-completeness}, supplies a derivation
from \(T_0\), hence from \(T\).
\end{proof}
\end{annexitem}

\begin{annexitem}{annex:p3.abstract.1}{thm:p03-robinson-joint-consistency}{Robinson joint consistency theorem}
\begin{proof}
Use first-order compactness and completeness under the ambient Choice
assumption.  In particular, consistency is equivalent to satisfiability,
and semantic consequences are derivable.

\paragraph{A complete common theory.}
For \(i=1,2\), let
\[
 C_i=\{\sigma\in\operatorname{Sent}(\Lang_0):T_i\models\sigma\},
 \qquad C=C_1\cup C_2.
\]
Every finite subset of \(C\) has a model.
Otherwise there would be finite conjunctions \(\alpha\) of members
of \(C_1\) and \(\beta\) of members of \(C_2\) such that
\(\models\beta\to\neg\alpha\).
Empty conjunctions here are \(\top\).
Then \(T_1\models\alpha\) and \(T_2\models\neg\alpha\), giving a
derivable common-language separator by completeness, contrary to
the hypothesis.
Compactness supplies a model \(A\models C\) in the common signature.
Let \(S=\operatorname{Th}_{\Lang_0}(A)\), a complete consistent theory.

For each \(i\), the union \(T_i\cup S\) is consistent.
If not, compactness would give a finite conjunction \(\delta\) of
members of \(S\) such that \(T_i\models\neg\delta\).
Thus \(\neg\delta\in C_i\subseteq S\), whereas \(\delta\in S\),
contradicting consistency of \(S\).
Choose models of both \(T_1\cup S\) and \(T_2\cup S\).
Their common reducts have complete theory \(S\).

\paragraph{Placing one reduct inside the other model.}
Start with a model \(M_0\models T_1\cup S\).
The set
\[
 T_2\cup S\cup
       \operatorname{ElDiag}_{\Lang_0}(M_0\mathbin{\upharpoonright}\Lang_0)
\]
is consistent in \(\Lang_2\) expanded by fresh constants for the
elements of \(M_0\).
Indeed, conjoin a finite diagram fragment into \(\delta(\bar c)\).
The sentence \(\exists\bar x\,\delta(\bar x)\) is true in
\(M_0\mathbin{\upharpoonright}\Lang_0\), hence belongs to \(S\).
A model of \(T_2\cup S\) therefore has witnesses for this fragment.
Interpreting its finitely many parameter constants by those witnesses
satisfies it together with the chosen theory sentences.
Compactness and the diagram test give a model \(N_0\models T_2\cup S\)
with an elementary embedding of \(M_0\mathbin{\upharpoonright}\Lang_0\) into its reduct.
Transport the structure along a bijection as in the preceding lemma
so that this embedding becomes an inclusion:
\[
 M_0\mathbin{\upharpoonright}\Lang_0\preccurlyeq N_0\mathbin{\upharpoonright}\Lang_0.
\]

\paragraph{Alternating elementary extensions.}
To bound the model choices in this recursion, fix an infinite cardinal
\(\kappa\) at least the size of \(N_0\) and of
\(\Lang_1\cup\Lang_2\).
Downward L\"owenheim--Skolem, Theorem~\ref{thm:downward-ls}, permits
each diagram model to have size at most \(\kappa\): its parameter
language has at most \(\kappa\) symbols.
Transport \(M_0,N_0\) together, placing the domain of \(M_0\) in
\(\kappa\times\{0\}\) and the remaining elements of \(N_0\) in
\(\kappa\times\{1\}\).
Place new elements at successive steps in unused blocks
\(\kappa\times\{2\},\kappa\times\{3\},\ldots\).
All subsequent choices therefore range over a fixed set of structures
on subsets of \(\kappa\times\mathbb N\); the ambient Axiom of Choice
suffices for the sequence.

Apply Lemma~\ref{thm:p03-elementary-reduct-extension} first to the
full \(\Lang_1\)-structure \(M_0\) and the common reduct of \(N_0\).
It yields a \(\Lang_1\)-structure \(M_1\) with
\[
 M_0\preccurlyeq M_1,\qquad
 N_0\mathbin{\upharpoonright}\Lang_0\preccurlyeq M_1\mathbin{\upharpoonright}\Lang_0.
\]
Apply it next to the full \(\Lang_2\)-structure \(N_0\) and the
common reduct of \(M_1\), obtaining \(N_1\) with
\[
 N_0\preccurlyeq N_1,\qquad
 M_1\mathbin{\upharpoonright}\Lang_0\preccurlyeq N_1\mathbin{\upharpoonright}\Lang_0.
\]
Continue recursively.  At each step, the transport in the lemma fixes
the entire preceding common reduct, so all these maps are literal
inclusions.  The resulting \(\Lang_1\)-structures form an elementary
chain \(M_0\preccurlyeq M_1\preccurlyeq\cdots\); the
\(\Lang_2\)-structures form an elementary chain
\(N_0\preccurlyeq N_1\preccurlyeq\cdots\).
Their common reducts interleave:
\[
 M_0\mathbin{\upharpoonright}\Lang_0\preccurlyeq N_0\mathbin{\upharpoonright}\Lang_0
 \preccurlyeq M_1\mathbin{\upharpoonright}\Lang_0\preccurlyeq N_1\mathbin{\upharpoonright}\Lang_0
 \preccurlyeq\cdots .
\]
In particular, the two chains have the same union of underlying domains.

Let \(M_\infty=\bigcup_n M_n\) and \(N_\infty=\bigcup_n N_n\).
The elementary chain theorem, Theorem~\ref{thm:elementary-chain},
gives \(M_\infty\models T_1\) and \(N_\infty\models T_2\).
Their common reducts agree.  For any finite tuple in the union domain,
choose an interleaved stage containing it; all later interpretations
of each common relation or function agree on that tuple because the
maps are embeddings.  Common constants agree for the same reason.
Consequently the union of the two compatible interpretations on this
one domain defines a \((\Lang_1\cup\Lang_2)\)-structure satisfying
\(T_1\cup T_2\), as required.

\paragraph{The complete-common-theory form.}
If both \(T_i\) extend a complete consistent \(\Lang_0\)-theory \(S\),
the no-separator hypothesis follows directly.
If \(T_1\models\sigma\) and \(T_2\models\neg\sigma\), completeness
of \(S\) puts either \(\sigma\) or \(\neg\sigma\) in \(S\).
One of the consistent \(T_i\) would then contain incompatible
consequences.  Conversely, the first part of this proof constructs
such an \(S\) compatible with both \(T_i\) from the no-separator
hypothesis.  Thus the two formulations give the same joint-consistency
principle.

\paragraph{Stone-space formulation of the first step.}
Complete \(\Lang_0\)-theories also form a Stone space with basic
clopen sets \([\sigma]=\{S:\sigma\in S\}\).
Compactness of this space is another form of first-order compactness:
if a cover by basic clopens has no finite subcover, the negations
of its defining sentences are finitely satisfiable, and a model
of all those negations gives a complete theory missed by the cover.
Every open cover refines to a cover by basic clopens.

Let \(X_i\) consist of complete common theories compatible with \(T_i\).
It is nonempty because \(T_i\) has a model, and is closed because an
incompatible complete theory has a finite conjunction witnessing
incompatibility.  The basic clopen defined by that conjunction
is disjoint from \(X_i\).
If \(X_1\) and \(X_2\) were disjoint, every point of \(X_1\) would
have a basic clopen neighborhood missing \(X_2\).
Compactness of \(X_1\) would select finitely many such neighborhoods.
Their union is one clopen \([\sigma]\), where \(\sigma\) is the
disjunction of their defining sentences.
Every \(T_1\)-model would satisfy \(\sigma\), and every
\(T_2\)-model would satisfy \(\neg\sigma\), contradicting the
no-separator hypothesis.
Hence \(X_1\cap X_2\) is nonempty, giving the same common theory
used by the elementary-chain construction.

\paragraph{Alternative model construction by ultrapowers.}
Once models \(M_i\models T_i\cup S\) have been chosen, their
\(\Lang_0\)-reducts are elementarily equivalent.
The Keisler--Shelah theorem,
Theorem~\ref{thm:p03-keisler-shelah}, supplies isomorphic ultrapowers
of those reducts.  Take the corresponding ultrapowers of the full
\(M_i\).  By \L o\'s's theorem they still satisfy \(T_i\), and
forming a reduct commutes with this ultrapower construction because
it uses the same domains, equivalence relation, and common-symbol
interpretations.
Transport the \(\Lang_2\)-interpretations along the common-reduct
isomorphism onto the domain carrying the first ultrapower.
They agree with its \(\Lang_1\)-interpretations on every common
symbol.  Their compatible union is again a joint model.
\end{proof}
\end{annexitem}

\begin{proof}

Theorem~\ref{thm:fol-compactness}, to this one defining sentence.

\begin{annexitem}{annex:p3.abstract.5}{thm:p03-craig-robinson-beth}{Craig--Robinson equivalence and Beth definability}
\begin{proof}
\paragraph{Craig interpolation implies joint consistency.}
Assume the Craig interpolation principle, and suppose
\(T_1\cup T_2\) is inconsistent.
Compactness supplies finite \(\Delta_i\subseteq T_i\) such that
\[
 \models A\to\neg B,\qquad
 A=\bigwedge\Delta_1,\quad B=\bigwedge\Delta_2.
\]
Empty conjunctions are \(\top\).
A Craig interpolant \(\sigma\) satisfies
\(\models A\to\sigma\) and \(\models\sigma\to\neg B\).
Every nonlogical symbol in \(\sigma\) occurs in both \(A\) and \(B\),
so belongs to \(\Lang_1\cap\Lang_2\).
Thus \(T_1\models\sigma\) and \(T_2\models\neg\sigma\).
Completeness converts these into the two derivable consequences
forbidden by the common-sentence hypothesis.
This proves Robinson's theorem from Craig interpolation and compactness.

\paragraph{Joint consistency implies sentence interpolation.}
Assume the common-sentence form of Robinson's theorem, and let
\(A,B\) be sentences with \(\models A\to B\).
If \(A\) is unsatisfiable, take the interpolant \(\bot\).
If \(B\) is valid, take \(\top\).
Otherwise \(\{A\}\) and \(\{\neg B\}\) are separately consistent,
and their union is inconsistent.
Give the first theory exactly the nonlogical occurrence signature of
\(A\), and the second exactly that of \(B\).
The contrapositive of Robinson's theorem supplies a sentence \(\sigma\)
in their common signature with
\[
 A\vdash\sigma,\qquad \neg B\vdash\neg\sigma.
\]
Soundness and classical contraposition yield
\(\models A\to\sigma\) and \(\models\sigma\to B\).
Logical equality and the truth constants are available regardless
of the nonlogical signature.  Hence \(\sigma\) is a Craig interpolant.

\paragraph{Free variables.}
For formulas \(A,B\), replace each variable free in either formula by
its own fresh constant symbol, obtaining sentences.
Validity under every assignment gives validity of the resulting
sentence implication under every interpretation of these constants.
The sentence argument produces an interpolant whose new constants
can come only from variables free in both original formulas.
Rename its bound variables and substitute the original variables
back for those constants.  The term and formula substitution induction
gives both original implications and the intersection condition on
free variables.  Repeated values of different parameters are allowed.

\paragraph{Beth definability.}
The proof in Annex~\ref{annex:p3.abstract.2} derives Beth definability
from Robinson's common-language separator using two renamed predicates.
Together with the first implication above, this also derives Beth
definability from Craig interpolation.
These are the implications stated in the theorem.
\end{proof}
\end{annexitem}

\begin{hbtheorem}{thm:p02-many-sorted-translation}{proved=annex:p2.hol.5}{Reduction of strict many-sorted consequence to one-sorted consequence}
Let \(\Lang_{\mathrm{MS}}\) be a strict many-sorted signature and let
\(\Gamma\cup\{\varphi\}\) be a set of well-sorted formulas.  Then
\[
 \Gamma\entails_{\mathrm{MS}}\varphi
 \quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
 \mathsf{Ax}_{\mathrm{sort}}(\Lang_{\mathrm{MS}})
   \cup\mathsf{VarGuard}_{\mathrm{MS}}(\Lang_{\mathrm{MS}})
   \cup\operatorname{tr}_{\mathrm{MS}}[\Gamma]
 \entails_{\mathrm{FOL}}
   \operatorname{tr}_{\mathrm{MS}}(\varphi).
\]
The left side uses nonempty pairwise-disjoint sort domains and same-sort
equality; the right side uses ordinary nonempty-domain first-order semantics.
\index{many-sorted first-order logic!reduction}
\end{hbtheorem}

\begin{annexitem}{annex:p2.hol.5}{thm:p02-many-sorted-translation}{Reduction of strict many-sorted consequence to one-sorted consequence}
\begin{proof}
First assume the one-sorted consequence fails under an assignment \(s\).  Let
\(\mathcal A\) satisfy \(\mathsf{Ax}_{\mathrm{sort}}(\Lang_{\mathrm{MS}})\),
\(\mathsf{VarGuard}_{\mathrm{MS}}(\Lang_{\mathrm{MS}})\), and every member of
\(\operatorname{tr}_{\mathrm{MS}}[\Gamma]\), but not
\(\operatorname{tr}_{\mathrm{MS}}(\varphi)\).  Put
\(M_{\mathsf s}\defeq Q_{\mathsf s}^{\mathcal A}\).  Nonemptiness and pairwise-disjointness
follow from the first and fourth axiom families; constant typing and function
closure make the restrictions of the old symbols well typed.  Restrict each
relation to the matching product of the \(M_{\mathsf s}\)'s.  Induction on terms, then
on well-sorted formulas, gives, for every matching assignment \(s\),
\[
 \mathcal M,s\entails\psi
 \quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
 \mathcal A,s\entails\operatorname{tr}_{\mathrm{MS}}(\psi).
\]
The atomic cases use the restrictions and same-sort equality; the guarded
quantifier clauses use exactly
\(M_{\mathsf s}=Q_{\mathsf s}^{\mathcal A}\).  The all-variable assignment
guard makes the given \(s\) a total matching sorted assignment, with no choice
of default values.  Thus the restricted many-sorted \(\mathcal M\) satisfies
\(\Gamma\) and refutes \(\varphi\).

Conversely, let a strict many-sorted \(\mathcal M,s\) satisfy \(\Gamma\) and
refute \(\varphi\).  Take the one-sorted domain to be the tagged union
\(\bigcup_{\mathsf s}\{\mathsf s\}\times M_{\mathsf s}\) together with one
fresh untyped point \(\star\), interpret
\(Q_{\mathsf s}\) by its \(\mathsf s\)-tagged
component, tag the assignment, and transport constants and correctly typed
function values.  Send every ill-typed positive-arity function input to
\(\star\), a simultaneous choice-free extension.
Interpret each relation by the transported correctly typed tuples and make it
false elsewhere.  The four sort-axiom families hold.  The same induction gives
truth preservation, so the resulting one-sorted structure satisfies the
translated premises and refutes the translated conclusion.  Taking
contrapositives in both directions proves the stated equivalence.
\end{proof}
\end{annexitem}

\begin{hbdefinition}{def:p08-negative-free-logic}{Negative free-logic semantics}
Fix a nonempty outer domain \(D^{\mathrm{out}}\), a nonempty existing domain
\(D^{\mathrm{in}}\subseteq D^{\mathrm{out}}\), and a total interpretation of
individual constants and function symbols into \(D^{\mathrm{out}}\).  In the
selected \emph{negative free-logic semantics}, each \(n\)-ary predicate has
extension contained in \((D^{\mathrm{in}})^n\),
\(E!(t)\) is true exactly when the value of \(t\) belongs to
\(D^{\mathrm{in}}\), and strict identity \(r=t\) is true exactly when both
term values exist and are the same object.  Quantifiers range over
\(D^{\mathrm{in}}\).  Hence every atom containing a denoting but nonexisting
outer-domain object is false; this is not called ``non-denotation.''

The adjective ``negative'' is necessary because positive free logic permits
some true predications of nonexisting objects, while a neutral partial
semantics can assign a truth-value gap when a term has no value.  It names one
two-valued model class, not all free logics.  Its strict atomic and equality
clauses distinguish it from the two exact variants in the table below and are
used by the guarded quantifier rules and description policy
\cite{Lambert1967,Bencivenga1986}.
\index{free logic}\index{negative free logic}\index{existence predicate}
\end{hbdefinition}

\begin{hbtheorem}{thm:p02-lomega-one-omega-calibration}{cited=Scott1965}{Basic \(L_{\omega_1\omega}\) calibration}
The language \(L_{\omega_1\omega}\) is not compact.  For every countable
structure in a countable signature there is an \(L_{\omega_1\omega}\)-sentence
whose countable models are exactly its isomorphic copies.  This Scott-sentence
claim is restricted to countable models; it is not blanket categoricity among
structures of every cardinality.
\end{hbtheorem}

\begin{hbtheorem}{thm:p02-karp-completeness}{cited=Karp1964}{Karp completeness boundary}
For the Karp infinitary calculus for \(L_{\omega_1\omega}\), semantic validity
implies derivability by a well-founded infinitary proof. This is weak
completeness for the declared semantics and proof objects; it does not restore
compactness, nor does it say that arbitrary semantic consequence from an
uncountable premise set has a countable subproof.
\end{hbtheorem}

For all \(\mathcal L\)-terms \(r,t,u\), every formula \(\varphi\), and every
variable \(x\), the natural-deduction equality rules on

 \varnothing\derives_{\mathsf{ND}_{\mathsf{FOL}}}t=t,
 \qquad
 \{r=t\}\derives_{\mathsf{ND}_{\mathsf{FOL}}}t=r,
\]
\[
 \{r=t,t=u\}\derives_{\mathsf{ND}_{\mathsf{FOL}}}r=u,
 \qquad
 \{r=t,\varphi[r/x]\}
   \derives_{\mathsf{ND}_{\mathsf{FOL}}}\varphi[t/x].
\]
Every displayed substitution is the total capture-avoiding operation of the
syntax chapter.  Reflexivity and replacement are the registered primitive
rules; symmetry and transitivity are derived, not silently added axioms.
\end{hbtheorem}

\begin{hbtheorem}{thm:p02-fol-clausal-form}{cited=BaazEglyLeitsch2001}{Clausal-form theorem}
For every first-order sentence \(\sigma\), there is a finite set \(S\) of
universally read clauses in a finite expansion of its signature such that,
assuming AC, \(\sigma\) is satisfiable iff \(S\) is satisfiable.  The reverse
direction from an \(S\)-model to a model of \(\sigma\) uses only reducts and
does not require choice.  The transformation is the composition in
Table~\ref{tab:p02-fol-normal-form-pipeline}; only the Skolem step weakens
same-signature logical equivalence to expansion--reduct equisatisfiability.
\end{hbtheorem}

\begin{hbtheorem}{thm:p02-fol-subformula-property}{cited=RathjenSieg2024}{Subformula property for cut-free first-order \(\mathsf{LK}\)}
In every derivation using neither Cut nor Mix on the equality-free registered
sheet \hyperref[sheet:lk]{\texttt{sheet:lk}}, every formula occurrence is a
first-order subformula instance of some formula occurrence in the endsequent.
In particular, the claim includes the term instances introduced by
\(\forall L\) and \(\exists R\), and the fresh eigenvariable instances
introduced by \(\forall R\) and \(\exists L\).  It is not the false claim that
every proof formula is a literal string-subformula of the endsequent, and it
does not apply to a derivation still containing Cut or Mix.
\end{hbtheorem}

\begin{hbtheorem}{thm:p03-keisler-shelah}{cited=Shelah1971Ultrapowers}{Keisler--Shelah isomorphism theorem}
For structures \(\mathcal M\) and \(\mathcal N\) in the same signature,
\(\mathcal M\equiv\mathcal N\) if and only if some ultrapower of
\(\mathcal M\) is isomorphic to some ultrapower of \(\mathcal N\).
No fixed index set, ultrafilter, nonprincipality condition, or cardinal bound
is asserted.  The reverse implication follows from \L o\'s's theorem and
isomorphism invariance; the forward implication is Shelah's theorem.
\end{hbtheorem}

actual_declarations.text:
\begin{hbtheorem}{thm:p03-compactness-ultraproduct}{proved=annex:p3.types.8}{Compactness via ultraproducts}
Assume the Axiom of Choice in the ambient set theory.  If every finite subset
of a set \(\Gamma\) of first-order \(\Lang\)-sentences is satisfiable, then
\(\Gamma\) is satisfiable.  The derivation in the annex uses the finite-subset
index set, extends its generated proper filter by the Ultrafilter Lemma, and
then applies \L o\'s's theorem; no choice-free claim is made.
\end{hbtheorem}

\begin{annexitem}{annex:p3.types.8}{thm:p03-compactness-ultraproduct}{Compactness via ultraproducts}
\begin{proof}
Let \(I\) be the set of finite subsets of \(\Gamma\).  By Choice, select for
each \(\Delta\in I\) a \(\Lang\)-structure
\(\mathcal M_\Delta\entails\Delta\).  For \(\sigma\in\Gamma\), put
\[
 I_\sigma=\{\Delta\in I:\sigma\in\Delta\}.
\]
The family \(\{I_\sigma:\sigma\in\Gamma\}\) has the finite-intersection
property: for \(\sigma_1,\ldots,\sigma_m\), the index
\(\{\sigma_1,\ldots,\sigma_m\}\) belongs to every corresponding
\(I_{\sigma_j}\).  Hence its upward, finite-intersection closure is a proper
filter.  The Ultrafilter Lemma extends it to an ultrafilter \(\mathcal U\).

For each \(\sigma\in\Gamma\), the generated filter and its extension give
\(I_\sigma\in\mathcal U\).  Every \(\Delta\in I_\sigma\) satisfies \(\sigma\),
so upward closure gives
\[
 I_\sigma\subseteq
 \{\Delta\in I:\mathcal M_\Delta\entails\sigma\},
 \qquad
 \{\Delta\in I:\mathcal M_\Delta\entails\sigma\}\in\mathcal U.
\]
By \L o\'s's theorem,
\(\prod_{\Delta\in I}\mathcal M_\Delta/\mathcal U\entails\sigma\).
This holds for every \(\sigma\in\Gamma\), so the ultraproduct is a model of
\(\Gamma\).
\end{proof}
\end{annexitem}
